title: Holy things without a Temple
hookLine: the fifth order: Temple offerings and kosher slaughter
carry: learning the offering counts as bringing it

cards: One tractate of the Mishnah reads like a builder's notebook. Gates and their names. Chambers and what each was for.
Courtyards, steps, the size of the altar, the places where priests kept watch at night. It's called Middot, measurements.
It belongs to the fifth of the Mishnah's six orders, beside tractates on animal offerings, grain offerings, birds, firstborn animals, and what happens when someone uses holy property for themselves.
No Temple stands today, and nobody brings these offerings. Yet students still open these pages.

teach.h: HOLINESS AS A STATUS: SET APART.
teach.b: Kodashim. Holy things. In the Mishnah, holiness works like a status.
An animal, a measure of flour, a coin: once it's dedicated to the Temple, it is set apart. It doesn't look different. It is different.
Three turns on that idea. First, misuse.

teach.h: ME'ILAH: DON'T USE IT AS ORDINARY.
teach.b: A whole tractate, Me'ilah, deals with someone who takes a holy thing and uses it as ordinary property. That's the danger: not dirt, but treating the set-apart as just another thing. Second, rhythm.
The tractate Tamid describes the daily offering, morning and evening, the Temple's steady heartbeat. One opinion in the Talmud says the daily prayers were set to match those offerings.
So a Jew praying the morning and afternoon services today is keeping time with a Temple clock. Third, study. With no Temple, what do you do with all these laws?
The Talmud, in the tractate Menachot, answers: whoever studies the law of an offering is counted as if they had brought it. The prophet Hosea had already pictured words offered in place of bulls.
So the pages became the altar.

teach.h: LEARNING IT COUNTS AS BRINGING IT.
teach.b: People learn the measurements of a building they've never seen, the way you might remember the layout of a grandparent's house. And tucked between the offerings is one more surprise, a tractate about ordinary meat.
That's tomorrow. For today: something becomes holy when it's set apart, and stays holy as long as it's treated that way.

how: Jews who study Talmud learn the order of Kodashim even though Temple offerings are not brought today, and some traditional prayer books include passages about the offerings in the morning service.

practice: In the Mishnah, a thing becomes holy by being set apart, so look for what you've set apart: an hour of the week, a ring, a letter in a drawer, a name you don't use lightly.
Hold one in mind, and ask the question of Me'ilah: when have I treated it as ordinary? No verdict; just notice where the line is.
